questions.q: To show 2n + 10 is O(n), which pair of constants works?
questions.e: We need 2n + 10 ≤ cn. With c = 3, this means 10 ≤ n, so n₀ = 10. With c = 2 it can never hold.

f(n) is both O(g(n)) and Ω(g(n))
questions.e: Slide 57's theorem: Θ is the intersection of O and Ω.

Results may not apply to inputs you did not test

questions.q: According to the Big-Oh rules, how should 3n + 5 be described?
questions.e: Use the simplest expression of the smallest class. O(n²) is true but not tight.

o: Big-O only applies to linear functions
n ≤ c would have to hold for a fixed c, and n grows without limit
No constant n₀ can be positive
n² is smaller than n for large n
questions.e: Dividing n² ≤ cn by n gives n ≤ c, which cannot hold for all large n.

questions.q: Algorithm A takes 100n steps and B takes 0.01n². For very large n:

questions.e: Little-o means f becomes insignificant relative to g.

questions.q: arrayMax runs in 7n − 1 operations. Why doesn't the 7 matter for its order?
o: Constants change only by a factor, not the growth rate
questions.e: T(n) is trapped between two linear functions, and constant factors don't alter growth rate.

questions.q: Prove that 4n² + 6n + 2 is O(n²), stating c and n₀.
questions.m: For n ≥ 1, 6n ≤ 6n² and 2 ≤ 2n², so 4n² + 6n + 2 ≤ 12n². Choose c = 12 and n₀ = 1.

questions.q: Give two reasons to prefer theoretical analysis over experiments.
questions.m: It does not require implementing the algorithm, it accounts for all possible inputs, and it is independent of hardware and software, so algorithms can be compared fairly.

questions.q: Explain what you must show to prove f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
questions.m: You must show both an upper bound, f(n) = O(g(n)), and a lower bound, f(n) = Ω(g(n)), giving constants c₁, c₂ and n₀ so that c₁g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂g(n) for n ≥ n₀.

questions.e: i takes values 1, 2, 4, 8..., so it reaches n after log₂ n steps.

questions.q: What is the complexity of two separate, consecutive loops, each running from 0 to n?
questions.e: Consecutive statements add: n + n = 2n, which is O(n).

questions.q: `p=0; for(i=1; p<n; i++) p=p+i;` runs in:
questions.e: p equals k(k+1)/2 after k iterations, so k is about √(2n).

questions.q: In `while (i <= n)` with i from 1, how many times does the test run?
questions.e: The final failing test counts, so one more than the body's n executions.

questions.q: Timing doubles from 6.4 s to 51.1 s as n doubles from 4,000 to 8,000. Likely order?
questions.e: The ratio is about 8, and 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Average comparisons for sequential search when x is present, with all positions equally likely:
questions.e: The average of positions 1 through n is (n+1)/2.

questions.q: `for(i=0;i<n;i++) for(j=0;j<i;j++) x++;` executes x++ how many times?
questions.e: j runs 0, 1, ..., n−1 times across the outer iterations, summing to n(n−1)/2.

questions.q: A recursive function does `f(n/2) + f(n/2)` plus constant work. Its complexity is:
questions.e: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c. The recursion tree's levels sum to about 2n nodes.

questions.q: Which rule applies to `if (a) O(1) else O(n)` in worst-case analysis?
o: O(n): test plus the larger branch
questions.e: Slide 16: never more than the test plus the larger of the two.

questions.q: Find the complexity of `for(i=0;i<n;i++) for(j=1;j<n;j=j*2) x++;` and justify it.
questions.m: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop doubles j, so it runs log n times. Nested loops multiply, giving O(n log n).

questions.q: State the four general rules for estimating running time.
questions.m: A loop costs its body times its iterations. Nested loops multiply all their sizes. Consecutive statements add. If/else costs the test plus the larger of the two branches.

questions.q: Explain how you would predict the runtime of 3-Sum at n = 16,000 from slide 8.
questions.m: Each doubling of n multiplies time by about 8, which suggests cubic growth. So 51.1 × 8 gives around 409 seconds at n = 16,000.

questions.q: Solve T(n) = T(2n/3) + 1.

questions.q: What is the solution of T(n) = T(n−1) + n?
questions.e: Summing n + (n−1) + ... + 1 gives n(n+1)/2.

questions.q: What is the solution of T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1?

questions.e: T(1)=1, T(2)=3, T(3)=7, which matches 2ⁿ − 1.

questions.q: Use the Master theorem to solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n log n. State a, b, the comparison and the case.
questions.m: a = 4 and b = 2, so n^(log₂4) = n². f(n) = n log n is polynomially smaller, so Case 1 gives T(n) = Θ(n²).

questions.q: Solve T(n) = n + 2T(n/2) by iteration, showing the pattern.
questions.m: After i expansions, T(n) = i·n + 2^i T(n/2^i). The expansion stops at i = lg n, giving n lg n + n T(1), which is Θ(n lg n).

questions.q: Describe the steps of the substitution method.
questions.m: Guess the form of the solution. State the induction goal with an unknown constant. Assume it holds for smaller inputs, substitute, and find values of the constant and n₀ that make the same inequality true.

questions.q: Show the first partition of 5 3 8 4 9 1 with the first element as pivot.
questions.m: Pivot is 5. From the left, 8 is ≥ 5; from the right, 1 is < 5. Swap to get 5 3 1 4 9 8. The searches cross, so swap the pivot with the last smaller value, 4, giving 4 3 1 5 9 8.

questions.q: Explain why quick sort becomes O(n²) on a sorted array when the first element is the pivot.
questions.m: Each pivot is the smallest element, so one partition is empty and the other has n−1 elements. The costs add up to n + (n−1) + ... + 2, which is O(n²).

questions.q: Derive the running time of merge sort from its three steps.
questions.m: Dividing is Θ(1), conquering is 2T(n/2) and combining is Θ(n). So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), which is Θ(n log n).

questions.q: Give a counterexample showing that greedy change-making isn't always optimal.
questions.m: With coins 1, 7 and 10 making 15, greedy takes 10 and five 1s, which is 6 coins. The optimal solution 7 + 7 + 1 uses only 3 coins.

questions.q: Explain why the greedy strategy is optimal for fractional knapsack.
questions.m: If a better solution used less of a high-ratio item and more of a lower-ratio item, swapping some of the lower-ratio item for the higher-ratio one would increase the benefit, which contradicts it being optimal.

questions.m: Sorted by profit: job 1 (50), job 2 (40), job 3 (30). Accept 1. Accept 2 as sequence [2, 1]. Job 3 has no free slot within its deadline. Total profit is 90.

questions.q: Explain the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a list.
questions.m: The while loop runs V times and finding the minimum scans V vertices, giving V². There are up to E updates at O(1). So the total is O(V² + E), which is O(V²).

questions.q: Explain why Dijkstra's algorithm can't be trusted with negative edges.
questions.m: A vertex is finalized on the assumption that no later route can be shorter. A negative edge could produce a shorter route after a vertex has been made final, so the greedy guarantee no longer holds.

questions.q: Describe how relaxation works when vertex v is finalized.
questions.m: For each unknown neighbour n, compute v's distance plus the edge weight. If it's smaller than n's distance, update n's distance and set n's previous vertex to v.

questions.q: Describe Kruskal's algorithm and how it avoids cycles.
questions.m: Start with each vertex as its own tree. Repeatedly take the cheapest remaining edge. If it would connect two vertices in the same tree it forms a cycle and is rejected; otherwise it merges two trees. Stop after n − 1 edges.

questions.q: Explain the main difference between Prim's and Kruskal's approach.
questions.m: Prim grows one connected tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge touching it. Kruskal considers the cheapest edge anywhere in the graph, building a forest whose trees merge over time.

questions.q: Define minimum spanning tree and give a real-world use.
questions.m: It is a subgraph that connects all vertices without cycles and has the smallest total edge weight. It is used to design networks such as cables or roads at the lowest cost.

questions.q: Write the recurrence for 0/1 knapsack and explain each case.

questions.q: Explain the meaning of each term in the matrix chain recurrence.
questions.m: For every split point k, the cost is the cost of the left chain m[i,k], plus the right chain m[k+1,j], plus multiplying the two results, p(i−1)·p(k)·p(j). The minimum over all k is the answer.

questions.q: What two properties must a problem have for DP to apply? Explain them.
questions.m: Optimal substructure: the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to smaller instances. Overlapping subproblems: the same subproblems recur, so storing their solutions avoids recomputation.

questions.q: Describe Karger's algorithm for min-cut.

questions.q: State the steps to prove that a problem is NP-complete.
questions.m: Show the problem is in NP with a polynomial-time verifier. Pick a known NP-complete problem. Reduce it to the new problem in polynomial time. By transitivity, every NP problem reduces to the new problem, so it is NP-complete.

questions.q: Explain the difference between P and NP.
questions.m: P contains problems that can be solved in polynomial time. NP contains problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time. Every P problem is also in NP.

questions.q: Why doesn't the O(nW) knapsack algorithm contradict knapsack being NP-complete?
questions.m: O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the numeric value of W, whereas the input size counts the bits needed to write W. So it is not polynomial in the input size.
